nature-eco-304.title: Ocean primary production: growth in the sunlit layer
nature-eco-304.text: In the sea, almost all new organic matter is made by algae. Ocean primary production happens in the photic zone, a sunlit surface layer about 10-100 m thick. That layer faces a constant drain. Sinking particles carry nutrients out of it, and they come back only when deeper water mixes upward or wells up. Some waters lack a single ingredient. Where wind-blown desert dust does not reach, as in the Southern and North Pacific oceans, a shortage of iron limits production. The result is high-nutrient, low-chlorophyll regions: plenty of other nutrients, but little of the green pigment that marks growing algae.

nature-eco-399.title: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium: the numbers on a fertilizer bag
nature-eco-399.text: A bag labeled 10-10-15 contains 10 percent nitrogen, 10 percent available phosphorus (P2O5) and 15 percent water-soluble potassium (K2O). Those three elements are the main plant nutrients added as fertilizer, and they are always listed in its analysis. Phosphorus that plants can actually absorb is the nutrient most often lacking, especially in humid tropical soils. Inorganic fertilizers are more concentrated than organic ones, and plants can use them immediately.

nature-eco-400.title: Soil depletion: spending the soil's nutrient bank
nature-eco-400.text: Soil fertility can be spent down like savings. Soil depletion is the loss of fertility when the things that make soil fertile are removed and not replaced. It brings poor crop yields, and it is becoming a global problem. Causes include overly intensive cultivation, over-tillage (too much plowing), salt build-up, and overuse of nutrient inputs that mines the soil's nutrient bank. Fertile soil is being depleted in many African farming regions, especially the Sahel, where population pressure is high.

nature-eco-325.title: Chemoautotrophs: life powered by chemistry, not sunlight
nature-eco-325.text: On the deep ocean floor, where no sunlight reaches, whole ecosystems run on chemistry. Their producers are chemoautotrophs: organisms that make food using energy from chemical reactions of inorganic substances instead of light. They are often found at deep-ocean hydrothermal vents, and they include some archaea and bacteria. They draw energy from substances such as hydrogen, iron, nitrogen and sulfur. This chemosynthesis is how producers make food in vent ecosystems without sunlight.

nature-eco-286.title: Ecosystem diversity: the variety of living systems
nature-eco-286.text: Insects that pollinate crops are worth $14.6 billion a year to the US economy. Doing the job by hand would cost $5,715-$7,135 more per hectare. Services like these depend on ecosystem diversity, the variety of ecosystems in a region or across the whole planet. It covers living features and non-living ones such as water and soil, on land and in water. Globally it spans deserts, forests, grasslands, wetlands and oceans, which makes it the largest scale of biodiversity. Diverse ecosystems help supply oxygen, purify water and provide plants used as medicines.

nature-eco-378.title: Survivorship curves: who dies young and who dies old
nature-eco-378.text: Some species lose most of their young almost at once, while others die mostly in old age. A survivorship curve shows the difference by graphing how many members of a population survive to each age. Type I curves, typical of most mammals, show deaths mostly late in life. Type II shows an equal chance of death at any age. Type III shows heavy early losses, then good survival for those that pass a certain age.

nature-eco-385.title: Do more plant species make a richer harvest?
nature-eco-385.text: Does a field with more plant species grow more? Ecologists have argued about it for a long time. Some research finds that productivity rises with diversity. Part of the reason is chance: more species make it likelier that a highly productive one is present. Other work finds a single peak, with productivity highest at middling diversity. One meta-analysis, a study pooling 44 earlier studies, found that peaked shape in all but one. A 1999 study of European grasslands found productivity rose with diversity and then leveled off. The question remains open.

nature-eco-384.title: Secondary production: building bodies from food
nature-eco-384.text: Animals, fungi and many bacteria build their bodies from what they eat. Secondary production is the creation of new biomass by these consumers from the food they assimilate, or absorb into their tissues. It is driven by organic material passing from one feeding level to the next. Measuring it takes care. Methods include increment summation, removal summation, the instantaneous growth method and the Allen curve method.

nature-eco-309.title: Conservation biology: a science with a deadline
nature-eco-309.text: Species may now be dying out about 1,000 times faster than the natural background rate. Conservation biology is the science that answers that loss. It aims to conserve nature and Earth's biodiversity, protecting species, habitats and ecosystems from excessive extinction. Because natural systems are declining so fast, it is often called a 'discipline with a deadline'. The field took its name from the First International Conference on Research in Conservation Biology, held in 1978 in La Jolla, California. It is interdisciplinary. It draws on the natural and social sciences and on the management of natural resources, and it reaches into law, economics and philosophy. Its methods come in two kinds. {{ref:nature-eco-131}} protects a species in its natural home, while {{ref:nature-eco-074}} works outside it, as in gene banks. Conservation biologists have also begun working with economists to measure nature's wealth and services, an accounting approach called natural capital. Values divide the field. Some conservationists follow a resource ethic of the greatest good for the most people. Others argue that nature has a worth of its own apart from its usefulness, the idea covered in {{ref:nature-val-056}}.

nature-eco-310.title: Indicator species: nature's early-warning signals
nature-eco-310.text: Amphibians have permeable skin and close ties to wetlands, so they are very sensitive to environmental harm. That makes them a 'miner's canary' for whole ecosystems. They are indicator species: species with narrow ecological needs whose condition is watched as a sign of an ecosystem's health. Such species are monitored to detect damage from pollution or other human activity. Their signals can guide changes in practice, such as forestry methods. Experts generally recommend watching several indicators, from genes to whole landscapes.

nature-eco-312.title: Systematic conservation planning: choosing where reserves go
nature-eco-312.text: Where should a new nature reserve go? Systematic conservation planning is a step-by-step way of choosing and designing reserves to protect the highest-priority biodiversity efficiently. Margules and Pressey set out six linked stages. They run from compiling biodiversity data and setting goals to selecting new areas and maintaining their value. Planners generally use computer mapping tools, described in {{ref:nature-es-051}}, to support their decisions.

nature-eco-294.title: Habitat: the place a species can live
nature-eco-294.text: The large blue butterfly lives only in chalk grassland, and only where certain ants live too. Its needs are narrow and exact. That set of needs is its habitat: the resources and the living and non-living conditions in a place that let a species survive and reproduce. Physical factors include soil, moisture, temperature range and light. Living factors include food supply and predators. A habitat can be seen as the physical form of a species' {{ref:nature-eco-281}}, its role in its surroundings. Species differ in how choosy they are. Generalists thrive in many conditions, while specialists like the large blue need a narrow set. Habitats on land include forests, grasslands, wetlands and deserts. Freshwater ones include rivers, lakes, marshes and bogs. Losing its habitat is the single greatest threat to any species. {{ref:nature-eco-041}} is the leading cause of the loss of species and of extinction worldwide. Protecting habitats, through national parks, reserves or limits on human activity, is a necessary step in keeping biodiversity. Not all tree cover counts. Plantations of a single tree species add trees but fail to provide the varied habitat most woodland creatures need.

nature-eco-281.title: The ecological niche: a species' address and its job
nature-eco-281.text: Every species has a role as well as a place to live. An ecological niche is the particular set of environmental conditions and the role that a species or population occupies in its surroundings. Roswell Hill Johnson coined the word in 1910, and Joseph Grinnell first used it in ecological research in 1917. For Grinnell, a niche was set by a species' habitat and the behaviors that let it persist and reproduce there. In 1927 Charles Elton defined it by an animal's place in the living world, especially its relations to food and enemies. A niche can be described along many axes, such as life history, habitat, feeding position and geographic range. Empty niches get filled. Introduced species may invade the niches of native organisms and outcompete them. Because every species evolved for a certain niche, {{ref:nature-hist-007}}, by shifting temperature and weather, puts species at risk.

nature-eco-331.title: Ecological communities: many species sharing one place
nature-eco-331.text: Two species can share a meadow only if they make their living in different ways. Each species occupies a niche, and having different niches lets species coexist. Together, the populations of different species living in the same area at the same time form a community. It is also called a biocoenosis, a biotic community or an ecological community. Community ecology studies how these coexisting species interact, and their distribution, structure and abundance. Some species carry outsized weight, among them the kinds described in {{ref:nature-eco-355}}, {{ref:nature-eco-301}} and {{ref:nature-es-086}}. Losing them often destabilizes the whole community. Ecologists often measure a community's structure through networks of who eats whom.

nature-eco-327.title: Biomes: the great living regions of Earth
nature-eco-327.text: Under {{ref:nature-hist-007}}, between 22% and 54% of land could end up with climates that match other biomes, and 3.6% with entirely new ones. A biome is a large geographical region with a distinctive climate, vegetation and animal life. Its community forms in response to its physical environment and regional climate. The International Biological Program of 1964–74 popularized the idea. Lines between biomes must be drawn somewhat arbitrarily, because one biome changes gradually into the next. Biomes can shift. Woody plant encroachment, which turns grass savanna into shrub savanna, is one example of a biome shift.

nature-eco-348.title: Ecological succession: how communities rebuild over time
nature-eco-348.text: Plow up a grassland and leave it, and it may need at least 100 years, and potentially 1,400 years on average, to regain its earlier biodiversity. That slow rebuilding is ecological succession: the way the mix of species in a community changes over time. It comes in two main kinds. {{ref:nature-eco-349}} starts on newly created ground with no life. {{ref:nature-eco-386}} follows a disturbance, such as a fire, that destroys an existing community. Succession drives itself. Growing plants cast shade, add organic matter to the soil and change the nutrient supply, which opens room for different plants. Early communities are dominated by fast-growing species that spread well. As a community nears its mature end point, or climax, the variety of species, plant biomass and stability rise. Net primary productivity and the speed of nutrient cycling fall. Two filters decide who succeeds at a site. One is whether seeds can reach it, called dispersal limitation. The other is whether they can survive there, called environmental filtering. Ecologists still debate how far chance, rather than predictable factors, sets the path of succession.

nature-eco-336.title: Competition: when two need the same scarce thing
nature-eco-336.text: Cheetahs and lions hunt the same prey and harm each other, yet both persist, against a prediction that one should push out the other. Competition, in biology, is an interaction in which organisms or species need the same resource, such as food, water or territory, when it is in limited supply. It lowers the fitness, the success at surviving and reproducing, of both sides. Each reduces what is left for the other. Competition within a species is intraspecific; competition between species is interspecific. Within a species it can regulate numbers. As a population grows, crowding leaves some individuals without enough. Competition is one force shaping community structure, the variety of species and the rise and fall of populations. In 1934 Georgii Gause proposed that species with the same ecological niche cannot coexist. The big cats show how messy the real world can be.

nature-eco-318.title: Wildlife conservation: keeping wild species alive
nature-eco-318.text: A 2019 UN report estimated that a million species are at risk of extinction. The IUCN, a global conservation body, counts over 42,100 assessed species at risk. Wildlife conservation is the practice of protecting wild species and their habitats, to keep wildlife populations healthy and restore natural ecosystems. The threats are many. Habitats are destroyed or broken into pieces, and species are overharvested, hunted illegally, polluted, squeezed by a changing climate and sold in illegal trade. More than 80% of the world's species live in forests, so forest clearing is a major threat. This illegal trade is estimated to be worth 7-23 billion, with around 100 million plants and animals traded a year. In 1973 the US passed its Endangered Species Act. Internationally, nations agreed {{ref:nature-mkt-001}} to stop global trade in wildlife at risk. Protecting a whole habitat is often the better choice when many species at risk share it. Monitoring populations lets managers track species at risk and test whether their work succeeds.

nature-es-086.title: Ecosystem engineers: species that build and reshape habitats
nature-es-086.text: Beavers fell trees and build dams, and in doing so they change the distribution and abundance of many other organisms. They are the original ecosystem engineer: a species that creates, substantially changes, maintains or destroys a habitat. Such species can strongly affect how many species an area holds and how varied its landscape is. They matter because they modify resources, not because they are eaten. Species covered in {{ref:nature-eco-301}} usually matter through feeding relationships instead. By making habitats more varied, beavers can support species not found elsewhere. Conserving one engineer may therefore protect a whole landscape's diversity. Whales release nutrients at the surface that feed phytoplankton and spread them across oceans, the {{ref:nature-eco-365}}. Introduced species such as kudzu and the zebra mussel often act as engineers. Humans are thought to be the most dramatic engineers of all, through cities, farming, logging, dams and mining. Some ecologists see the term as a buzzword, since it may imply intent and every species changes its environment to some degree.

nature-eco-285.title: Competitive exclusion: complete competitors cannot coexist
nature-eco-285.text: 'Complete competitors cannot coexist.' That blunt summary is sometimes called Gause's law. The competitive exclusion principle holds that two species competing for the same limited resource cannot both persist at steady numbers. A species with even a slight advantage dominates in the long run. The weaker competitor dies out or shifts to a different niche. The principle has real-world force. Species described in {{ref:nature-eco-026}} can drive native species locally extinct this way. Not everyone accepts its reach. Ecologists Andrewartha and Birch argued that most natural populations rarely exhaust their resources, so putting too much weight on competition is wrong.

nature-eco-386.title: Secondary succession: how life returns after fire
nature-eco-386.text: Knobcone pine cones open only when a forest fire heats them. For some species, destruction starts the cycle. Secondary succession is the succession that follows an event such as fire, harvesting or a hurricane. The event knocks back an existing ecosystem but leaves soil and some life in place. That head start makes it usually faster than {{ref:nature-eco-349}}, because soil, seeds, roots and underground plant parts survive. Consider an oak–hickory forest after wildfire. Annual plants, which live a single season, come first. Grasses and pioneer species follow, then shrubs and young trees. Over about 150 years the forest returns to a stable mature community resembling the one before the fire. The rebuilding reaches underground too. Succession from Imperata grassland to regrown forest raises the carbon stored in the soil.

nature-eco-335.title: Interspecific interactions: who gains and who loses
nature-eco-335.text: Rhizobium bacteria live in nodules on legume roots, and both partners gain. That is one of several ways species can affect each other. Interspecific interactions are the ways different species affect one another, classed by whether each side gains, loses or is unaffected. {{ref:nature-eco-366}} benefits both sides, as with Rhizobium. In commensalism one species benefits and the other is unaffected, like an orchid growing on a tree. In amensalism one species harms another while staying unaffected itself. Tadpoles do this to snails by eating the algae the snails need. {{ref:nature-eco-380}} and {{ref:nature-eco-369}} benefit one species at the other's expense. Competition harms both. True neutralism, where neither species is noticeably affected, is rare, because communities are so interconnected.

nature-eco-369.title: Parasitism: living on, and off, a host
nature-eco-369.text: Almost every free-living animal hosts at least one parasite species. Vertebrates alone host between 75,000 and 300,000 species of helminths, or parasitic worms. Parasitism is a close relationship in which one organism, the parasite, lives on or in another, the host, and harms it. Parasites range from the protozoans that cause malaria to hookworms, lice, fungi such as honey fungus, and plants such as mistletoe. Parasitic plants make up about one per cent of flowering plants and occur in almost every biome. Unlike organisms that break down dead matter, parasites feed on living hosts. Their burden is lopsided: most hosts carry few parasites, while a few hosts carry the great majority. Farmers put parasites to work. Parasitoid wasps and microbial pathogens serve as biological control agents in agriculture.

nature-eco-366.title: Mutualism: partnerships where both sides win
nature-eco-366.text: In Three Sisters farming, beans climb cornstalks while fixing nitrogen for the corn. Both crops come out ahead. Mutualism is an interaction between species in which each gains a net benefit. It contrasts with competition, where both lose fitness, and with parasitism, where one benefits at the other's expense. Examples are common: plants trading with fungi, the carrying of pollen between flowers, fruit-eating animals spreading seeds, and corals living with zooxanthellae algae. In {{ref:nature-eco-397}}, a partnership of fungus and root, the plant gives the fungus carbohydrates in return mainly for phosphate. Rhizobia bacteria fix nitrogen for legumes in return for carbohydrates. Such deals are not permanent. Mutualism can evolve from parasitism or commensalism, and it can break down again.

nature-eco-284.title: Niche differentiation: how competitors learn to share
nature-eco-284.text: Some lizard species seem to share the same ground by eating insects of different sizes. That is niche differentiation: the process by which competing species use their environment in different ways, which helps them live side by side. It is also called niche segregation, niche separation or niche partitioning. Species that split their niches compete less strongly, so they are more likely to coexist. Without such splitting, {{ref:nature-eco-285}} predicts that one competitor would push out the other. Dividing up food, as the lizards do, is one form, called resource partitioning. The differences can arise in three ways: from competition today, from the past extinction of weaker competitors, or from species evolving different patterns of resource use. The pattern is not universal. One group of hispine beetles shares the same food and habitat with no evidence of niche differentiation. Differences can even add up to more than the parts. Plants living together can play complementary roles, such as cycling nutrients and regulating water, a mechanism called niche complementarity.
